Dystrophin function influences a clinical spectrum

Diagnostic or treatment principle

  • In-frame variants often produce a Becker phenotype, but exceptions occur.
    • Duchenne more often has severe protein disruption.
    • Genotype-phenotype interpretation is not absolute.

Applying the principle

  • Do not under-monitor the heart in mild skeletal disease.
    • Offer appropriate family and carrier assessment.
    • Use genetic confirmation rather than the age label alone.

Key distinctions

Finding or strategyInterpretation
DuchenneUsually severe early muscle disease
BeckerOften partial protein function
BothCardiac surveillance needed

Other Options

  • Becker never involves the heart: Cardiomyopathy can be clinically important.
  • Becker is an acquired autoimmune disorder: It is part of the inherited dystrophinopathy spectrum.
  • Normal walking ability excludes every dystrophinopathy: Mild and cardiac-predominant phenotypes occur.

Diagnostic or treatment principle

  • A coordinated team can anticipate complications and reduce fragmented decisions.
    • Symptoms and caregiver needs change over time.
    • Palliative support can coexist with active treatment.

Applying the principle

  • Use ongoing shared planning.
    • Discuss ventilation, feeding and communication preferences at an appropriate pace.
    • Provide caregiver and bereavement resources when relevant.

Key distinctions

Finding or strategyInterpretation
TeamMultiple functional domains
Palliative careCan begin alongside active treatment
PlanningRevisited over time

Other Options

  • Avoid discussing preferences because prognosis is uncertain: Uncertainty makes supported planning important rather than irrelevant.
  • A prescription-only pathway without follow-up: ALS needs changing multidisciplinary support.
  • Palliative care only in the final hours: Symptom and goal-focused care can be helpful much earlier.

questions.explanationHtml:
Describe the level of diagnostic certainty

Diagnostic or treatment principle

  • CIS identifies a first clinical demyelinating event when MS criteria are not yet met.
    • Additional MRI, CSF or follow-up evidence may change classification.
    • Under current criteria some people can meet MS criteria after a first event.

Applying the principle

  • Do not equate one attack with low future risk.
    • Risk depends on the lesion and biomarker pattern.
    • Discuss follow-up and treatment options with a specialist.

Key distinctions

Finding or strategyInterpretation
CISFirst clinical event, criteria not yet met
RISIncidental radiological presentation
MSCriteria-defined diagnosis

Other Options

  • Radiologically isolated syndrome despite an objective clinical event: RIS describes an incidental radiological presentation without a prior attributable clinical event.
  • Definite MS solely because the patient is young: Age does not substitute for diagnostic evidence.
  • Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: That is a peripheral demyelinating disorder.

Clock timing and sleep ability are different dimensions

Diagnostic or treatment principle

  • A diary and actigraphy can reveal a stable delayed pattern.
    • Exclude insufficient sleep, shift work and other explanations.
    • The preferred-schedule response is informative.

Applying the principle

  • Use a timing-aware treatment plan.
    • Light and melatonin effects depend on timing and the diagnosis.
    • Seek sleep expertise rather than random bedtime dosing.

Key distinctions

Finding or strategyInterpretation
TimingDelayed
Preferred scheduleSleep can be relatively normal
AssessmentLongitudinal diary/actigraphy

Other Options

  • Severe OSA is proven by late bedtime alone: Timing does not establish respiratory obstruction.
  • Long-term sedative escalation is the only possible intervention: Schedule and circadian strategies may be relevant.
  • The person necessarily has no genuine impairment: Conflict with work or school can be disabling.
